strengths: Addresses an important and practically motivated problem in online advertising: coordination among multiple auto-bidders maximizing value subject to Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints, moving beyond the isolated individual-agent view predominant in prior literature.

The theoretical characterization in Theorem 3.1 is sharp and elegant, establishing Assumption 1 (competitive highest coalition values relative to outside bids) as both necessary and sufficient for the simple highest-value-compete mechanism to strictly reduce RoS violation for every bidder.

Theorem 4.1 provides a strong, unconditional asymptotic guarantee showing that coordinated mirror-descent auto-bidders always achieve weakly higher total value than independent mirror-descent auto-bidders, regardless of whether Assumption 1 holds.

The paper is well-written and mathematically rigorous, providing complete proofs, addressing boundary cases (e.g., dual multiplier converging to zero), and extending the core results to asymmetric/non-i.i.d. value distributions.
Empirical evaluations on both synthetic setups and semi-synthetic simulations using the public iPinYou dataset nicely corroborate the theoretical findings.
weaknesses: The coordination protocol requires full revelation and centralized comparison of exact private values across all coalition members at every auction round. While plausible for a single advertiser managing multiple internal campaigns, it faces incentive and privacy hurdles when independent advertisers form a coalition without an elicitation mechanism.

Outside competition is assumed to be an exogenous, stationary i.i.d. distribution $D$. In realistic auction ecosystems, outside competitors are also dynamic auto-bidders whose equilibrium reactions could alter the gains from collusion.

Unlike the utility bounds in Theorem 3.1 which feature explicit finite-horizon dependencies ($T \Delta / N$), the value domination results in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.2 are asymptotic as $T \to \infty$; explicit finite-time convergence rates for the value gap would further strengthen the theory.

In the non-i.i.d. setting (Section 5), coordination only guarantees welfare gains at the coalition-aggregate level rather than Pareto improvements for each individual participant, necessitating an internal redistribution/transfer mechanism that is not formalized.

strengths: The paper addresses a very relevant and timely problem in modern online advertising: coordination among multiple auto-bidding agents/campaigns with Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints. While prior literature largely focuses on utility maximizers or independent bidding, analyzing value maximizers fills an important conceptual gap.

The theoretical characterization of RoS violation reduction is elegant: Assumption 1 provides an interpretable necessary and sufficient condition on the value and outside bid distributions under which coordination reduces RoS violation for all weakly overbidding algorithms.

The analysis for mirror-descent auto-bidders is rigorous and comprehensive, showing asymptotic total value improvement over independent bidding unconditionally (Theorem 4.1) and asymptotic optimality among all coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1 (Theorem 4.2).

The authors provide extensions to non-i.i.d. valuations and substantiate the theoretical findings with clean numerical simulations on synthetic distributions as well as semi-synthetic evaluations using the public iPinYou dataset.
weaknesses: The assumed coordination mechanism requires exact centralized knowledge of all participating bidders' private valuations in every round before bidding. In many agency or multi-advertiser scenarios, private valuations may be proprietary or require elicitative mechanisms.

In Theorem 4.2, the coalition multipliers converge to zero because expected utility is strictly positive under Assumption 1, causing bids to blow up to infinity and win all items. While theoretically correct within the dual mirror-descent framework, this implies the RoS constraint becomes completely slack, effectively trivializing the value maximization into winning every auction. A deeper discussion on the economic implications and practical constraints (e.g., maximum bid caps) would strengthen the paper.

The outside competition is assumed to be an exogenous i.i.d. bid $d^O$. In realistic auction markets, outside bidders also use adaptive auto-bidding algorithms, which can create non-stationary feedback loops when facing a coordinated coalition.

For the non-i.i.d. setting, the coordination mechanism does not guarantee individual rationality (some coalition members may be worse off individually), and surplus redistribution mechanisms are left as an open challenge.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: While the auto-bidding literature predominantly studies individual bidders, and traditional auction collusion literature focuses on utility maximizers, this work provides a formal treatment of coordinated bidding among value-maximizing agents subject to Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints.

Solid theoretical contributions: The paper establishes rigorous guarantees for a simple yet natural coordination protocol (highest-value bidder competes): Theorem 3.1 characterizes utility/RoS improvements via Assumption 1, and Theorem 4.1 establishes that mirror-descent auto-bidders achieve weakly higher coalition value under coordination without distributional assumptions.

Comprehensive mathematical proofs: The appendix provides extensive and careful proofs, including a non-trivial potential function drift analysis under mirror descent dynamics and thorough handling of the boundary case where the dual multiplier converges to zero (Appendix B.2).

Extensions to asymmetric settings: Section 5 extends the analysis to independent but non-identically distributed valuations (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2), identifying sufficient conditions (Assumption 2) for value dominance in asymmetric coalitions.
weaknesses: Artificial construction for the necessity claim in Theorem 3.1: The negative direction in Theorem 3.1 relies on a trigger-strategy auto-bidding algorithm (Appendix A.2) that artificially monitors whether the bidder was instructed to bid zero in the past and switches to bidding the maximum possible bid forever. Because realistic learning auto-bidders (e.g., mirror descent, dual averaging) do not employ retaliatory trigger rules, claiming Assumption 1 is a necessary condition for coordination to help auto-bidders is practically unconvincing.

Strong informational requirement on the coordinator: Algorithm 2 assumes the central coordinator has access to the exact realized valuations of all coalition members at every auction round prior to bidding. While plausible for a single firm managing an internal campaign portfolio (Scenario 2), it is impractical for a third-party agency coordinating distinct advertisers (Scenario 1) without an elicitation mechanism, as independent advertisers would have incentives to misreport their values to be chosen as the active bidder.

Exogenous, stationary outside competition: The model assumes outside bids are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed stationary distribution. In real advertising exchanges, outside participants are also adaptive auto-bidding agents. Coordinated bid suppression could significantly alter external bidders' pacing and multiplier dynamics, an effect not captured here.

Semi-synthetic empirical evaluation: The experiments on the real-world iPinYou dataset are essentially semi-synthetic simulations. Because the dataset only contains winning prices without private valuations or coordination labels, the authors sample values i.i.d. from the empirical winning price distribution and generate outside bids by multiplying values by a uniform random factor U[1, 2]. This limits the degree to which the empirical results reflect true market dynamics.

Absence of platform revenue and market welfare analysis: The coordination mechanism operates by suppressing internal competition (setting all non-highest coalition bids to zero), which directly reduces the clearing price paid to the auctioneer. The paper does not analyze the impact on publisher/platform revenue or discuss the anti-competitive/antitrust ramifications of deploying such collusive coordination protocols in practice.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical open problem in online advertising: coordinating multiple auto-bidders under Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints, moving beyond the predominant independent-agent paradigm.

Strong and rigorous theoretical contributions: the paper establishes a clean necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1) on value and outside-bid distributions for coordination to reduce RoS constraint violations for all overbidding algorithms.

Proves asymptotic optimality: Theorem 4.1 establishes that coordinated mirror-descent auto-bidders always achieve weakly higher total value than independent mirror-descent bidders without distributional assumptions, and Theorem 4.2 proves that under Assumption 1 it achieves the best possible coalition value among all conceivable coordination mechanisms.
Clear extensions to asymmetric / non-i.i.d. valuations with formal guarantees on coalition-level utility and value.
Well-written, logically structured, and mathematically thorough, with complete proofs covering both interior and boundary multiplier dynamics.
weaknesses: The coordination protocol assumes centralized access to true valuations $v_{i,t}$ to select the highest-value bidder $i^* = \arg\max_i v_{i,t}$ each round. While natural for a single advertiser managing multiple campaigns, in multi-advertiser agency coalitions this raises private-information elicitation and incentive compatibility questions.
The market environment assumes exogenous, stationary i.i.d. outside competing bids $d_t^O \sim D$, abstracting away strategic or learning responses from external auto-bidders.

The real-world experiment on iPinYou is essentially a semi-synthetic simulation (sampling values from pooled winning prices and scaling outside bids by $U[1, 2]$), rather than an end-to-end counterfactual evaluation on authentic auction traces.
Minor presentation flaw: broken cross-reference on page 9 ('coordinated mirror descent algorithms (?? 3)').

strengths: Addresses an important and practical open problem in online advertising auctions: while most auto-bidding literature assumes independent bidding, multi-campaign coordination by agencies or multi-brand conglomerates (e.g., Amazon, Temu) is prevalent in real markets.

Provides a sharp, necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1, $\Delta \ge 0$) under which coordination guarantees reduced RoS constraint violation (increased utility) across all overbidding auto-bidding algorithms (Theorem 3.1).

Establishes strong, distribution-free value dominance results for the standard class of mirror-descent auto-bidders (Theorem 4.1), and demonstrates that coordinated mirror descent achieves the optimal total value across all possible coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1 (Theorem 4.2).
Theoretical arguments are mathematically rigorous and elegant, leveraging potential functions, dual envelope upper bounds, and virtual bidder reductions.
Extensions to asymmetric, non-i.i.d. valuations are thoughtfully analyzed (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2), showing that coalition-level welfare improvements are robust to heterogeneity.
Theoretical findings are well-supported by numerical simulations on both synthetic distributions and semi-synthetic experiments based on the public iPinYou dataset.
weaknesses: The outside competition is modeled as an exogenous, i.i.d. random variable $d_t^O \sim D$, which abstracts away strategic feedback and adaptive learning dynamics from competitors outside the coalition.

The coordination mechanism requires complete, truthful sharing of realized values $v_{i,t}$ within the coalition prior to bidding. In settings where coalition members are distinct advertisers managed by an intermediary, incentive compatibility for reporting private values is not addressed.

Under Assumption 1 ($\Delta > 0$), the asymptotic optimality of coordinated mirror descent stems from the multipliers decaying to zero, driving bids to infinity and winning every round because average utility remains positive. In practical advertising platforms, spend pacing and round-by-round budget constraints typically prevent unconstrained overbidding.

The empirical evaluation on the iPinYou dataset is semi-synthetic: because bidder identities and coalition structures are not recorded in the log, values are drawn i.i.d. with replacement from the pool of winning prices, rather than testing on genuine auction coordination traces.

strengths: Novel and relevant problem formulation: While the auto-bidding literature predominantly studies independent bidding or utility-maximizing agents under budget constraints, this paper investigates coordinated bidding for value-maximizing auto-bidders subject to Return-on-Spend (RoS) constraints, addressing practical scenarios such as multi-campaign management and advertising agency coalitions.

Sharp characterization of RoS violation (Theorem 3.1): The paper identifies a clean, intuitive necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1, Delta >= 0) on the value and outside-bid distributions under which coordination reduces RoS violation for every member of the coalition across any overbidding algorithm. The counterexample construction for the necessity direction is rigorous and insightful.

Strong value-dominance guarantees for mirror descent (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2): The authors prove that coordinated mirror descent unconditionally dominates independent mirror descent in total value as T -> infinity. Moreover, under Assumption 1, coordinated mirror descent is proved to achieve the theoretical upper bound across all possible coordination mechanisms.

Rigor and technical soundness: The theoretical analysis of the mirror descent dynamical system—leveraging Legendre mirror maps, Bregman divergences, Lyapunov-style potential functions, and dual envelope relaxations—is thorough and mathematically solid.

Clear writing and transparent discussion of limitations: The paper is structured logically, provides clear economic intuition behind key assumptions (e.g., proving that Assumption 1 holds for sufficiently large N), and openly discusses extensions and limitations in Sections 5 and 7.
weaknesses: Information and incentive assumptions within the coalition: Algorithm 2 assumes that the central coordinator perfectly observes the realized private valuations of all coalition members at every round. While this model fits a single advertiser coordinating multiple internal ad campaigns, it overlooks internal incentive compatibility and strategic misreporting when distinct advertisers coordinate through a third-party agency.

Exogenous modeling of outside competition: The outside competing bid is assumed to be i.i.d. drawn from a stationary distribution D. In practical ad exchanges, competing outside bidders often employ their own auto-bidding algorithms, whose dynamic responses to coalition behavior could alter the equilibrium dynamics.

Semi-synthetic nature of the empirical evaluation: In the experiments on the iPinYou dataset (Section 6.1.2), valuations are generated by resampling from the aggregate pool of winning prices and outside bids are scaled synthetically. While understandable given public dataset limitations, this setup is closer to a calibrated synthetic simulation than a true trace-driven real-world evaluation.

Restrictive assumptions for the asymmetric setting: In the non-i.i.d. valuation setting (Section 5), coordination only guarantees aggregate RoS improvement rather than individual Pareto improvement, and the value optimality result requires Assumption 2 (Delta_i > 0 for all bidders), which requires every coalition member to have positive expected margin upon winning.
